1:1.t: 2 Timothy is probably Paul's last letter, written from prison in Rome shortly before his death.

1:5.t: Timothy's mother was Jewish and his father Greek (Acts 16:1).

3:8.t: Jannes and Jambres: Jewish tradition gives these names to Pharaoh's magicians (Exodus 7:11).

4:6.t: "Poured out like a drink offering": a drink offering of wine was poured out on or beside a sacrifice; Paul pictures his coming death this way. See Philippians 2:17.

4:10.t: Dalmatia: part of Illyricum, on the east coast of the Adriatic.

4:11.t: Mark, once rejected by Paul (Acts 15:37-39), is now "helpful".

4:13.t: "Scrolls ... parchments": the KJV's "books ... parchments", perhaps copies of the Scriptures.

4:14.t: "May the Lord repay him": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "the Lord will repay him".

4:19.t: "Priscilla": the KJV's "Prisca", the shorter form of her name (Romans 16:3).

4:22.t: "Jesus Christ": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read only "The Lord".

1:7.t: "Self-discipline" (Greek sophronismos): the KJV's "a sound mind", self-control, sound judgment.

1:12.t: "What I have entrusted ... the good deposit" (Greek paratheke): a deposit left in safekeeping. Paul entrusts his life to God; Timothy must guard the gospel entrusted to him.

1:14.t: "What I have entrusted ... the good deposit" (Greek paratheke): a deposit left in safekeeping. Paul entrusts his life to God; Timothy must guard the gospel entrusted to him.

2:15.t: "Correctly handles" (Greek orthotomounta): the KJV's "rightly dividing", literally "cutting straight", like a road cut straight or a craftsman's straight cut.

3:16.t: "God-breathed" (Greek theopneustos): the KJV's "given by inspiration of God". Scripture is breathed out by God, its source. "All Scripture" meant first the Old Testament (3:15); Christians apply it to the New Testament as well (compare 2 Peter 3:16).

4:7.t: "Fought the good fight ... finished the race": pictures from athletic contests; Paul often pictures the Christian life as a race. See Acts 20:24.

4:8.t: "Crown" (Greek stephanos): the victor's wreath, not a royal crown.
